newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela, Mbeki bolster Zaire peace initiative.
newsitem.headline: Mandela, Mbeki bolster Zaire peace initiative.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela and his deputy Thabo Mbeki are pulling out the stops to pursue their Zaire peace initiative and ensure a shipboard summit goes ahead on Wednesday, officials said.

Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela was scheduled to chair the second face-to-face meeting between President Mobutu Sese Seko and his rebel rival, Laurent Kabila, aboard the South African navy ice-breaker Outeniqua in the Congo port of Pointe Noire at 11 a.m. (1000 GMT) on Wednesday.
"There is no reason to believe that the meeting will not go ahead. Everything is on track," Mankahlana told Reuters.
He said Mandela had been telephoning other African leaders regularly over the past week, including the presidents of Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Gabon and Congo, to solicit their backing.
Responding to speculation in South Africa and Zaire that the prospects for a settlement were waning, Mankahlana said:
"The fact that we are going to Congo tomorrow is indication enough that we believe it is possible to find a solution."

He said Mandela would not comment directly on reports from Lubumbashi that Kabila, whose forces control three quarters of Zaire, had reneged on a promise to halt his advance on the capital at least until after his second meeting with Mobutu.

"Our understanding is that all parties are committed to the negotiation process. Until Kabila sends President Mandela a formal note saying he no longer feels bound by his undertaking, we have to assume he is sticking to his promise," he said.
Zaire's information minister, Kin-Kiey Mulumba, said after a special cabinet meeting that the front line was around Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) from the capital.
"The fighting is very violent," he told state radio. "The FAZ (Zairean Armed Forces) are busy maintaining the front line and pushing it back."
The rebels, who admit facing stiff resistance, have been talking tough ahead of Wednesday's meeting and Mankahlana said at least some of their statements could be pre-talks rhetoric.
Ricky Naidoo, a spokesman for Mbeki, said the deputy president was "tentatively" scheduled to fly to Zaire on Tuesday afternoon to see Mobutu in Kinshasa and Kabila in Lubumbashi.
"We are all on standby to go. The deputy president wants to make sure that there is some agreement in place before they go onto the ship tomorrow," he said.
Mbeki told reporters on Monday that Wednesday's meeting could be the last chance to avoid a bloody showdown in Kinshasa.

He said diplomatic initiatives would be geared towards advance agreement on the mechanism of a transition to democracy after 32 years of autocratic rule by Mobutu, the role that he and Kabila would play and the timetable for change.
Mankahlana said Mandela accepted that some loose ends might remain to be tied up after Wednesday's summit, but said it was important that the major issues should be agreed.
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga, told Belgian RTL-TVI television his father was ready to make serious concessions.
Kabila, leader of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, has continued to insist he will meet Mobutu only to discuss his departure from office.
